hook.text: Interval training is sold on fat loss.
Pool the trials, rate how far each result can be trusted, and the order flips.

populationPanel.text: Who was studied: 1,130 adults with a mean age of 26.27 years, across thirty-six randomized trials lasting 3 to 15 weeks.
Most were inactive and overweight or obese, so the findings describe that group best.
Children, teenagers and people with a known disease were left out.

paragraphs.text: Picture your weight as two piles on one scale.
One pile is fat; the other is everything else: muscle, bone, organs, blood and water.
A bathroom scale reads only the two together.
The second pile has a name: fat-free mass.
Interval training means bursts of hard work with rests between them.
In these trials, interval training moved the two piles in opposite directions.
Compared with no exercise, the fat pile shrank by 1.86 kg on average, and the other pile grew by 0.51 kg.
So a bathroom scale would show less than what changed underneath.

headline.text: In these trials, interval training moved them in opposite directions.

figure.alt: Two panels, before and after 3 to 15 weeks of training, each with a standing outline beside two stacked blocks: fat below, everything else above. After training, the fat block is marked less, on average, and the other block a little more, on average. The blocks are drawn the same size in both panels, because the paper gives no sizes. Below, two strips show two ways to build a session: short hard bursts with short easy rests, and long bursts with long still rests. The authors found the first pattern more effective.

paragraphs.text: The trials compared interval training with no exercise, for 3 to 15 weeks.
Then the authors rated how far they could trust each result.
Fat-free mass rated high, fat mass moderate and body fat percentage low.
Some settings kept coming out ahead.
More than 8 weeks, three sessions a week, bursts under 60 seconds, and rests of 90 seconds or less, spent moving.
These leads come from comparing groups of trials, not from testing one setting against another.
For fat-free mass, only cycling showed a clear gain; running did not.

effect.text: Fat-free mass: 0.51 kg more than with no exercise, pooled across the trials.

weakEnd.text: The 95% confidence interval for fat-free mass runs from 0.06 kg to 0.95 kg.
At its weak end, 0.06 kg is an amount no bathroom scale would register.
High certainty means the trials agree that the average is above zero, not that it is big.

limitations.text: Most trials enrolled inactive adults who were overweight or obese.
People who already train may respond differently.
The trials disagreed with one another, most of all on body fat percentage, which is why the authors graded it low.
The trials measured body composition in different ways, from skinfold calipers to DEXA scans.
Take one trial out and the fat-free-mass result is no longer clear.

missed.text: Leave that trial out and the estimate becomes 0.46 kg lost, ranging from 1.38 kg lost to 0.44 kg gained.
So the best-graded result also rests on a single study.

more.text: Cycling’s fat-free-mass gain was 0.63 kg (95% CI 0.17 to 1.09).
Overground running showed the widest drop in body fat percentage, 2.80 points (95% CI 3.89 to 1.71), on the outcome graded low.
Treadmill running showed no clear difference in fat mass: from 2.82 kg lost to 0.62 kg gained.
An earlier pooled analysis found no clear effect of cycling on fat mass in overweight and obese adults.
Heavier bodies load the joints differently when running, one reason cycling may suit some people.

glossary.plain: Everything in your body that is not fat: muscle, bone, organs, blood and the water in and around your cells. A body scan can split your weight into fat and this rest; an ordinary bathroom scale cannot.
Exercise in bursts of hard work, with rests between them.
Chance decided who did the training and who did not, not the researchers.

wewege.quote: a systematic review and meta-analysis by Wewege et al. [] found no significant effect of cycling on measures of body composition (whole-body FM) in overweight and obese adults

concepts.plain: Everything in your body that is not fat: muscle, bone, organs, blood and the water in and around your cells. A body scan can split your weight into fat and this rest; an ordinary bathroom scale cannot.
concepts.model: Two piles on the scale: a fat pile and a pile of everything else. An ordinary bathroom scale only reads the two together.

reference.title: The five-level model: a new approach to organizing body-composition research

daytime-caffeine-sleep.text: The schedule tested was three doses, the last one 475 minutes after waking, which came 8 hours before bed.
The finding covers a steady daily habit.
The authors caution that it may not hold after several days without caffeine.
Bedtime at home drifted about 25 minutes later on caffeine, so watch the clock as well as the cup.

hiit-body-composition.text: If lean mass is the aim, the supported combination in these trials was cycling intervals, three sessions a week, for more than 8 weeks.
Keep work bursts to 60 seconds or less: longer bursts showed no clear gain in fat-free mass, with an interval from 2.28 kg lost to 0.57 kg gained.
Standing still between bursts showed no clear gain in fat-free mass.
Two sessions a week did not clearly change body fat percentage; three did.

steps-days-per-week.text: If a daily target keeps failing, the study's lowest active group is a reasonable place to start: 8,000 steps on 1 to 2 days a week.
Past 3 to 4 such days the association flattened, so a missed day is no reason to write off the week.
The association was widest in adults aged 65 and over, at 19.9 points against 7.4 points in younger adults.

turmeric-pepper-breakfast.text: The dose tested was 1 g of black pepper, cooked into the egg of a toast-and-tea breakfast.
The glucose difference showed 30 minutes after eating and not in the 3-hour total.
Turmeric alone, at 1 g, showed no clear difference in glucose.
